name: Roman London Bridge
notes: Timber piled bridge built c. AD 50 by the founders of Londinium; probably destroyed in the Boudican revolt (AD 60) and rebuilt. Position approximate - archaeological pier evidence lies slightly downstream (east) of the modern bridge, near Fish Street Hill / Pudding Lane. Length, width, deck height and both dates all highly uncertain (?); the c.400 death date is the conventional end of Roman Londinium, not a recorded demolition (?). A succession of Saxon and Norman timber bridges occupied roughly the same site between c.400 and 1209 and are not separately entered here (?).

name: Old London Bridge
notes: Begun 1176 by Peter of Colechurch, completed 1209. Nineteen pointed stone arches on massive timber-piled piers with protective starlings, a central drawbridge (last opened in the 1470s) and the Chapel of St Thomas. Carried houses and shops up to seven storeys until the London Bridge Act 1756; houses demolished 1758-1761 and the two central arches replaced by one 'Great Arch' in 1758-62. Closed and demolished 1831-32 after New London Bridge opened. Sat about 30 m downstream (east) of the modern alignment, on the line of Fish Street Hill; coordinates derived from that offset (?). Deck height above mean water approximate (?).

name: New London Bridge (Rennie)
notes: Designed by John Rennie the Elder, built by his son John Rennie the Younger; opened 1 August 1831. Five semi-elliptical arches of Haytor granite, built 100 ft (30 m) upstream (west) of the medieval bridge. Widened 1902-04 to about 20 m, which contributed to its settling. Sold 18 April 1968 to Robert P. McCulloch, dismantled 1968-1971 and the facing stones re-erected at Lake Havasu City, Arizona. Death year given as 1967 (closure to traffic / start of replacement); physical removal completed 1971 (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: London Bridge
notes: Prestressed concrete box girder, three spans, longest span 104 m. Architect Lord Holford, engineers Mott, Hay and Anderson. Built 1967-72 on the site of Rennie's bridge and opened by Elizabeth II on 16 March 1973. Cost GBP 4 million, funded by Bridge House Estates. Deck height above mean water approximate (?).

name: Tower Bridge
notes: Combined bascule and suspension bridge, engineer John Wolfe Barry with architect Horace Jones. Construction from 22 April 1886, opened 30 June 1894. Total length 940 ft (290 m) including abutments; central bascule span 200 ft (61 m); towers 65 m high. Clearance 8.6 m (29 ft) above high water when closed, 42.5 m (135 ft) when open. Steel frame clad in Cornish granite and Portland stone. High-level walkways converted from cantilever to suspension form in 1960. Deck height above mean water estimated from the quoted high-water clearance (?).

name: Cannon Street Railway Bridge (Alexandra Bridge)
notes: Built 1863-66 for the South Eastern Railway, engineers John Hawkshaw and John Wolfe Barry, opened 1866. Originally five wrought iron spans carrying five tracks on cast iron cylinder piers. Widened to ten tracks and about 120 ft (37 m); the rebuilt bridge reopened 13 February 1892. Further strengthened 1913 with six new 443 ft girders, and the deck was renewed in the 1980s. Some sources date the bridge 1866 and others 1883 or 1892 for the widened structure (?). Width quoted is post-widening; original width about 24 m (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Southwark Bridge (Rennie)
notes: Designed by John Rennie the Elder, built 1814-19 and opened 1819 as a toll bridge. Three cast iron arches on granite piers, the 240 ft (73.2 m) centre span being the longest cast iron span ever built. Cost GBP 700,000; fifty men died in construction. Known as the 'Iron Bridge' and appears in Dickens's Little Dorrit. Closed 1913 and demolished to make way for the present bridge; demolition ran into the First World War (?). Length and width approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Southwark Bridge
notes: Steel arch bridge designed by architect Ernest George and engineer Basil Mott, built by Sir William Arrol & Co. Opened by King George V on 6 June 1921. Five spans, longest 240 ft (73.2 m). Carries the A300. Grade II listed; maintained by Bridge House Estates for the City of London Corporation. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Millennium Bridge
notes: Steel lateral suspension footbridge with cables below deck level ('blade of light'), by Arup, Foster + Partners and Anthony Caro. Opened 10 June 2000, closed after two days on 12 June 2000 because of synchronous lateral excitation ('wobbly bridge'), reopened 22 February 2002 after fitting 37 viscous and 52 tuned mass dampers at a cost of GBP 5 million. Three spans of 81 m, 144 m and 108 m. Classified here as footbridge although structurally a shallow suspension bridge. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Blackfriars Railway Bridge (first, St Paul's)
notes: Designed by Joseph Cubitt for the London, Chatham and Dover Railway, opened 1864; five wrought iron arch spans on cast iron columns, with heavy abutments bearing the LCDR insignia. Became too weak for modern trains and its deck was removed in 1985, leaving the red-painted cast iron piers standing in the river and the Grade II listed southern abutment with its LCDR crest. Immediately upstream (west) of the 1886 bridge; coordinates derived from that offset (?). Length and width approximate (?). rebuilt_as points to the 1886 bridge as functional successor, but the two coexisted 1886-1985.

name: Blackfriars Railway Bridge
notes: Wrought iron bridge built by Lucas and Aird, engineers John Wolfe Barry and Henry Marc Brunel, opened 1886 with St Paul's station (renamed Blackfriars 1937). Five spans: two middle spans of 185 ft, shore spans 183 ft, secondary spans 175 ft. Clear width 81 ft (24.7 m) between parapets, widening to 123 ft at the northernmost span. Rebuilt and extended 2009-2012 to carry the Thameslink Blackfriars station across the whole river, with a solar-panel roof. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Blackfriars Bridge (Mylne)
notes: Designed by Robert Mylne in an Italianate style, built 1760-69 and opened as a toll bridge in 1769; originally named William Pitt Bridge. Nine semi-elliptical arches of Portland stone, 995 ft (303 m) long. Tolls abolished 1785. Weakened by scour after the removal of Old London Bridge changed the tidal regime; some sources say dismantling began in 1860 and others give demolition in 1864 (?). Width approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Blackfriars Bridge
notes: Five wrought iron arches designed by Joseph Cubitt, opened by Queen Victoria on 6 November 1869. Originally 70 ft (21 m) wide; widened between 1907 and 1910 to 105 ft (32 m) to take trams, making it one of the widest bridges in London. Carries the A201. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Waterloo Bridge (Rennie)
notes: Designed by John Rennie the Elder, opened 18 June 1817 on the second anniversary of the battle; originally to be called Strand Bridge. Nine semi-elliptical arches of 120 ft span separated by paired Doric columns, in Cornish granite. 1,240 ft (378 m) between abutments, 2,456 ft (748.6 m) including approaches - length_m here is the river structure. Toll bridge until nationalised in 1878. Piers settled badly from 1923; closed and demolished from 1936, the demolition being publicly controversial. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Waterloo Bridge
notes: Designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, construction begun 1937. Reinforced concrete box girders clad in Portland stone, five spans, longest 233 ft (71 m). Partially opened 11 March 1942 and fully complete in 1945 (formally opened 10 December 1945); birth year given as 1942 for the first opening, 1945 for full completion (?). Built largely by a female workforce, hence 'The Ladies' Bridge'. Grade II* listed 1981. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Hungerford Suspension Footbridge (Brunel)
notes: Designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel to serve Hungerford Market, opened 1 May 1845. Central span 676 ft (206 m) with two side spans; Italianate brick towers. Bought in 1859 by the Charing Cross Railway Company and demolished in 1860-62 to make way for the railway bridge; the wrought iron chains were re-used on Brunel's Clifton Suspension Bridge in Bristol, and the brick piers were partly reused. Total length and width approximate (?). Death year 1860 marks the start of removal (?).

name: Hungerford Bridge (Charing Cross Railway Bridge)
notes: Wrought iron / steel lattice truss railway bridge designed by Sir John Hawkshaw, opened 1864 to carry the South Eastern Main Line into Charing Cross station. Replaced Brunel's suspension footbridge and reused its piers. Originally carried narrow pedestrian walkways on both sides, later only the downstream one, until the Golden Jubilee Bridges replaced them. A three-year refurbishment of the truss metalwork began in January 2025. Length and width approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Golden Jubilee Bridges
notes: A pair of cable-stayed pedestrian decks flanking the 1864 Hungerford railway bridge on either side, designed by Lifschutz Davidson Sandilands with WSP Group; opened 2002 and named for the Golden Jubilee of Elizabeth II. Sources give the length variously as about 300 m or 325 m (?). Coordinates are for the pair as a whole - the two decks sit roughly 20 m either side of the rail bridge centreline (?). Carry about 8.5 million pedestrians a year, London's busiest footbridges. Width per deck approximate (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Westminster Bridge (Labelye)
notes: Designed by the Swiss engineer Charles Labelye, built 1739-50 and opened 18 November 1750; the second bridge in central London after London Bridge, famously the subject of Wordsworth's sonnet of 1802. Fifteen semicircular stone arches on caisson-founded piers, about 1,223 ft (373 m) long with a roadway around 30 ft wide inside a total width of about 44 ft (?). Subsided badly and was expensive to maintain; replaced in stages and finally removed in 1861 (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Westminster Bridge
notes: Seven cast iron arches by engineer Thomas Page with Gothic detailing by Charles Barry to harmonise with the new Palace of Westminster; opened 24 May 1862. 820 ft (250 m) long, 85 ft (26 m) wide. Painted green to match the benches of the House of Commons. Grade II* listed 1981. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Lambeth Bridge (Barlow)
notes: Designed by Peter W. Barlow, opened 10 November 1862 as a toll bridge on the site of the ancient Lambeth horse ferry. 828 ft (252.4 m) long. Widely disliked and structurally poor; badly corroded, it was closed to vehicles by 1910 and used only by pedestrians before demolition around 1929 to make way for the present bridge. Width and deck height approximate (?). Death year 1929 approximate (?).

name: Lambeth Bridge
notes: Five-span steel arch bridge by engineer Sir George Humphreys with architects Sir Reginald Blomfield and G. Topham Forrest, built by Dorman Long; opened by King George V on 19 July 1932. Painted red to match the benches of the House of Lords. Obelisks at each end topped with stone pine cones (popularly but wrongly called pineapples). Grade II listed 2008. Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Vauxhall Bridge (Regent Bridge)
notes: The first iron bridge over the Thames, designed by James Walker after an abandoned stone design by John Rennie; opened 4 June 1816 as Regent's Bridge, later Vauxhall Bridge. Nine cast iron arches on stone piers, about 809 ft (247 m) long. Toll bridge until bought by the Metropolitan Board of Works in 1879. Piers undermined by tidal scour; demolition began in 1898 with a temporary timber bridge alongside from August 1898 until 1906. Width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Vauxhall Bridge
notes: Five steel arches on granite piers, designed by Sir Alexander Binnie and modified by Sir Maurice Fitzmaurice; opened 26 May 1906 by the Prince of Wales. 809 ft (247 m) long, 80 ft (24 m) wide. The first Thames bridge to carry trams. Eight large bronze figures by Alfred Drury and Frederick Pomeroy added on the piers in 1907. Grade II* listed 2008. Carries the A202. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Grosvenor Bridge (Victoria Railway Bridge)
notes: The first railway bridge across the Thames in central London, built 1859-60 by the Victoria Station and Pimlico Railway for GBP 84,000 to carry two tracks into Victoria; engineer Sir John Fowler. Widened by four tracks on the east side 1865-66 (engineer Sir Charles Fox, GBP 245,000), and again in 1907 with a further track on the west side for the LBSCR. In 1963-67 the whole superstructure was renewed by Freeman Fox & Partners, leaving only the cores of the original piers, and a tenth track added. Now nine tracks, Network Rail. Structurally a series of iron/steel arches rather than lattice trusses; kind set to rail_lattice as the nearest category (?). Width given is the modern width; the 1860 bridge was about 12 m wide (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Chelsea Bridge (Victoria Bridge)
notes: Designed by Thomas Page, built 1851-58 and opened 3 April 1858 as Victoria Bridge; renamed Chelsea Bridge as its structural weakness became known. 703 ft (214 m) long, 47 ft (14 m) wide with a 32 ft roadway and 7.5 ft footpaths; central span 333 ft (101 m). Wrought iron deck with ornate cast iron towers. Demolished 1934-37; death year given as 1935 as the mid-point of demolition (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Chelsea Bridge
notes: The first self-anchored suspension bridge in Britain, with the suspension cables anchored into the deck rather than into ground anchorages; designed by G. Topham Forrest and E. P. Wheeler for the LCC. Opened 6 May 1937. 698 ft (213 m) long, 64 ft (20 m) wide with a 40 ft roadway and cantilevered 12 ft pavements; central span 332 ft (101 m). All-steel construction. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Albert Bridge
notes: Opened 23 August 1873, designed by Rowland Mason Ordish on his patented Ordish-Lefeuvre cable-stayed system with 32 inclined stays. 710 ft (220 m) long, 41 ft (12 m) wide, original central span 384 ft 9 in (117.27 m). Strengthened by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1884-87 with conventional suspension chains, and again in 1973 when the GLC added two concrete piers mid-river turning the centre into a simple beam - so it is now a hybrid of three bridge types. Nicknamed 'the Trembling Lady'; troops are ordered to break step. Grade II* listed. Closed in February 2026 for repairs to cracked cast iron (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Old Battersea Bridge
notes: Timber toll bridge on the site of the Chelsea-Battersea ferry, opened to pedestrians in November 1771 and to vehicles in 1772. 734 ft (224 m) long, 24 ft (7.3 m) wide, with 19 narrow spans (widest 32 ft) that boats struck constantly. Painted repeatedly by Whistler and Turner. Two spans were replaced by iron girders in 1873 to ease navigation. Closed and demolished 1885. kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category available - this was an 18th century timber trestle, not a Roman bridge. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Battersea Bridge
notes: Five cast iron arches on granite piers designed by Sir Joseph Bazalgette, opened 21 July 1890. 725 ft 6 in (221.13 m) long, 40 ft (12 m) wide, longest span 163 ft (50 m). The narrowest and one of the busiest road bridges in central London; frequently struck by river traffic. Carries the A3220. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Battersea Railway Bridge (Cremorne Bridge)
notes: Opened to traffic 2 March 1863 for the West London Extension Railway; engineer William Baker. Originally the Cremorne Bridge (after Cremorne Gardens), also Battersea New Bridge, and officially Chelsea River Bridge to Network Rail. Five wrought iron arches flanked by brick approach viaducts: 230 m over the river, 387.1 m overall; longest span 42.5 m. Carries the West London Line (London Overground Mildmay line). The most complete survivor of the six 1860s Thames railway bridges; Grade II* listed 2008. Structurally arched rather than lattice; kind set to rail_lattice as the nearest rail category (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Wandsworth Bridge (Tolme)
notes: Wrought iron lattice truss road bridge on five spans by Julian Tolme, opened 26 September 1873 at a cost of GBP 40,000. Only 30 ft (9.1 m) wide, a commercial failure as a toll bridge, freed from tolls in 1880. Weight-restricted from 1935 and demolished in 1937. kind set to rail_lattice to capture the lattice-truss form although it was a road bridge. Length and deck height approximate (?).

name: Wandsworth Bridge
notes: Three-span steel cantilever bridge by Sir Thomas Peirson Frank, opened 25 September 1940 at a cost of about GBP 503,000. 650 ft (200 m) long, 60 ft (18 m) wide, clearance 39 ft (11.9 m) at lowest astronomical tide - deck_height_m here is referred to mean water level, so lower (?). Painted dull blue as wartime camouflage and still blue. Carries the A217; about 53,000 vehicles a day.

name: Fulham Railway Bridge (Putney Railway Bridge)
notes: Opened 3 June 1889, designed by William Jacomb (Brunel's former assistant) and built by Head Wrightson for the London and South Western Railway. 418 m total with five river spans covering 301 m. Lattice girder construction. Carries the London Underground District line between Putney Bridge and East Putney, with a public footway on the downstream (east) side. Refurbished 1995-97. Colloquially 'the Iron Bridge'; it has no official name. Width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Fulham Bridge (old Putney Bridge)
notes: Timber toll bridge authorised by the Fulham and Putney Bridge Act 1725, built by the carpenter Thomas Phillips to designs by Sir Jacob Ackworth, Surveyor of the Navy; opened 29 November 1729. For many years the only bridge between London Bridge and Kingston. About 786 ft (240 m) long on 26 narrow timber piers, with tollbooths at each end; two spans replaced by a single iron span in 1870-72 to ease navigation. Bought by the Metropolitan Board of Works in 1879, tolls ended 1880, demolished after the new bridge opened in 1886. Stood roughly 30 m downstream (east) of the present bridge, aligned on Putney and Fulham parish churches; coordinates derived from that offset (?). kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category available. Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Putney Bridge
notes: Five-arch stone and granite bridge designed by Sir Joseph Bazalgette, opened 29 May 1886 by the Prince and Princess of Wales. 700 ft (210 m) long and originally 43 ft (13 m) wide; widened in 1933 to three carriageways, so the modern width is about 22 m (?). Marks the start of the Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race course. Grade II listed; maintained by Wandsworth Council. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Hammersmith Bridge (Tierney Clark)
notes: The first suspension bridge over the Thames, designed by William Tierney Clark and opened 6 October 1827 at a cost of GBP 80,000. 822 ft 8 in (250.75 m) total with 688 ft 8 in (209.91 m) of clear waterway and a 688 ft (210 m) main span; wrought iron bars, stone towers, timber roadway with granite surfacing. Carriageway 20 ft (6.1 m) plus two 5 ft footways. Overloaded by 11,000-12,000 spectators at the 1870 Boat Race, prompting replacement; closed 1884 and replaced by a temporary bridge during construction of the present one. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Hammersmith Bridge
notes: Suspension bridge by Sir Joseph Bazalgette using the original 1827 pier foundations, built by Dixon, Appleby & Thorne and opened 11 June 1887 at a cost of GBP 82,117. 700 ft (210 m) long, 43 ft (13 m) wide, main span 400 ft (120 m), in steel and wrought and cast iron with ornate painted ironwork. Grade II* listed. Closed to motor traffic in April 2019 after cracks were found in the cast iron pedestals, and closed entirely August 2020 - February 2021; still restricted. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Barnes Railway Bridge (Locke, original)
notes: Designed by Joseph Locke for the Richmond and Windsor Railway, built from 1846 by Fox Henderson & Co and opened 22 August 1849. Two pairs of cast iron arch spans of 36.57 m with a rise of 3.66 m, six ribs each 915 mm deep, on brick piers faced with Bramley Fall stone, carrying a timber deck. Superseded in 1895 but the arches physically survive alongside the newer bridge on the upstream side, disused. Coordinates offset slightly upstream of the 1895 bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Barnes Railway Bridge
notes: Built 1894-95 to a design by Edward Andrews, contractor Head, Wrightson & Co, alongside and downstream of Locke's 1849 arches which remain in place. Three spans of wrought iron bowstring girders on extended piers and abutments, with a 2.4 m wide pedestrian footpath. Carries the Hounslow Loop line. Grade II listed 1983. Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Chiswick Bridge
notes: Opened 3 July 1933 by the Prince of Wales on the same day as Twickenham Bridge and the rebuilt Hampton Court Bridge. Architect Sir Herbert Baker, engineer Alfred Dryland. 606 ft (185 m) long, 70 ft (21 m) wide, five spans (three over the river, two over towpaths), longest span 150 ft (46 m); reinforced concrete faced with 3,400 tons of Portland stone. At completion the longest concrete span over the Thames. Near the Boat Race finish. Structurally a concrete arch; kind set to concrete_beam as the nearest category (?). Deck height approximate (?).

name: Kew Railway Bridge
notes: Opened 1 January 1869 between Kew and Strand-on-the-Green, Chiswick; engineer W. R. Galbraith, builders Brassey & Ogilvie, for the London and South Western Railway. 575 ft (175 m) long, five spans of about 35 m, wrought iron lattice girders on cast iron piers. Carries two electrified tracks used by the London Overground Mildmay line and the London Underground District line. Grade II listed 1983. Width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Kew Bridge (first, Tunstall)
notes: Opened 1 June 1759, designed by John Barnard and built by Robert Tunstall as a toll bridge replacing the Kew ferry. Two stone arches at each end with seven timber arches between; over 3,000 people crossed on the opening day. Lasted only 30 years because of the cost of maintaining the timber spans. Stood a short distance downstream of the later bridges; coordinates approximate (?). kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Kew Bridge (Paine)
notes: All-stone bridge designed by James Paine, opened 22 September 1789 by George III. About 1,000 ft (305 m) long including approaches with a 56 ft roadway; seven arches. Tolls abolished in 1873 when the Metropolitan Board of Works bought it. Too narrow and steep for growing traffic; closed and demolished around 1898-1902 for the present bridge - death year 1898 approximate (?). Width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Kew Bridge (King Edward VII Bridge)
notes: Officially the King Edward VII Bridge, opened 20 May 1903 by Edward VII. Designed by John Wolfe-Barry and Cuthbert Arthur Brereton. 1,182 ft (360 m) long, 75 ft (23 m) wide, three granite arches (Kemnay Quarry, Aberdeenshire), largest span 133 ft. Carries the A205 South Circular between Hounslow and Richmond upon Thames. Grade II listed 1983. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Richmond Lock and Footbridge
notes: Half-tide lock, weir and footbridge opened 19 May 1894 by the Duke of York (later George V), built to hold water upstream after the removal of Old London Bridge lowered the tidal river. 250 ft (76.2 m) long, 26 ft 8 in (8.1 m) wide, with five ornate metal arches. Three vertical steel sluice gates each weigh 32 tons and measure 66 ft by 12 ft; they are raised into the footbridge superstructure at high tide. Chief engineer F. G. M. Stoney, ironwork by Ransomes & Rapier of Ipswich. The only Thames lock operated by the Port of London Authority. Grade II* listed. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Twickenham Bridge
notes: Opened 3 July 1933 by the Prince of Wales. Architect Maxwell Ayrton, engineer Alfred Dryland. Three reinforced concrete arches on concrete piers with Art Deco bronze cover plates, balustrades and lamps; the first reinforced concrete bridge in the UK to use three permanent hinges to accommodate thermal movement. Carries the A316 Chertsey Road between Richmond and St Margarets. Site of the UK's first Gatso speed camera in 1992. Grade II* listed 2008. Structurally a concrete arch; kind set to concrete_beam as the nearest category (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Richmond Railway Bridge
notes: Opened 1848, designed by Joseph Locke and J. E. Errington; among the first railway crossings of the Thames. Three spans totalling 91.5 m. The original cast iron arches were replaced in situ with steel by John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood in 1906-08, reusing the piers and abutments and reproducing the 1848 appearance; deck and girders renewed again in 1984. Treated here as one continuous structure rather than split into 1848 and 1908 entries (?). Carries National Rail between Richmond and St Margarets. Grade II listed 2008. Width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Richmond Bridge
notes: The oldest surviving Thames bridge in London. Built 1774-77 by James Paine and Kenton Couse to replace a ferry, opened to traffic 12 January 1777 and completed December 1777; a toll bridge until 1859. 300 ft (91 m) long, five elliptical Portland stone arches of varying height with a humpbacked profile and a tall 60 ft central span for shipping. Widened by about 11 ft and slightly flattened in 1937-40. Grade I listed. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Kingston Railway Bridge
notes: Opened 1863 for the London and South Western Railway; the original cast iron structure was replaced by the present steel bridge in 1907 by John Wykeham Jacomb-Hood, treated here as one continuous structure (?). Five spans, three over the river and two over land, with two piers in the water; deck about 22 ft 4 in (6.81 m) above the water. Carries the Kingston Loop line between Kingston and Hampton Wick stations. Length and width approximate (?).

name: Kingston Bridge (medieval timber bridge)
notes: A timber bridge existed at Kingston from at least 1193 and probably earlier; for centuries it was the only Thames crossing between London Bridge and Staines. Described as dangerously decayed in 1318, damaged in the Wars of the Roses, repeatedly patched and eventually condemned in the early 1800s. Birth year 1190 is a nominal date for a bridge first documented in 1193 (?). It stood a short distance downstream of the present bridge, near the mouth of the Hogsmill; coordinates approximate (?). kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Kingston Bridge
notes: Classical Portland stone bridge by Edward Lapidge, county surveyor of Surrey; foundation stone laid by the Earl of Liverpool 7 November 1825, opened by the Duchess of Clarence 17 July 1828. Five elliptical arches, originally 382 ft (116.43 m) long and 27 ft (8.2 m) wide with a 60 ft centre span. Widened on the downstream side 1912-14 to 55 ft, and again in 2000 to 79 ft (24.08 m) for cycle and bus lanes - width given is the modern width. Carries about 50,000 vehicles a day on the A308. Grade II* listed 1951. Deck height approximate (?).

name: Teddington Lock Footbridges
notes: A pair of iron footbridges designed by G. Pooley, built 1887-89 with money raised by local subscription and opened in 1889. The southern bridge is a suspension span over the weir stream from Teddington to a small island; the northern bridge is an iron girder span from the island over the lock cut to Ham on the Surrey bank. Both Grade II listed since 3 October 2005. Maintained by Richmond upon Thames Council. This is the tidal limit of the Thames. Length given is the combined crossing including the island; individual span lengths, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Hampton Court Bridge (first)
notes: Built 1752-53 by Samuel Stevens and Benjamin Ludgator, opened 13 December 1753. Seven timber arches in an elaborate Chinoiserie style reflecting the fashionable Willow pattern; a toll bridge. Structurally weak and short-lived. kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Coordinates assumed the same as the present bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Hampton Court Bridge (second)
notes: Replacement timber bridge of eleven arches, sturdier and plainer than its Chinoiserie predecessor; opened 1778. By the 1840s it was condemned as 'crazy, hog-backed, inconvenient and obstructive of the navigation'. kind set to roman_timber as the only timber category. Coordinates assumed the same as the present bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Hampton Court Bridge (third)
notes: Built 1864-65 with wrought iron lattice girders resting on four cast iron columns. Highly profitable as a toll bridge, taking over GBP 3,000 a year, but widely condemned as 'one of the ugliest bridges in England'. Tolls ended 1876 when Surrey and Middlesex county councils bought it. Demolished for the present bridge in 1933. kind set to rail_lattice to capture the lattice-girder form although it was a road bridge. Coordinates assumed the same as the present bridge (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Hampton Court Bridge
notes: Designed by W. P. Robinson with Sir Edwin Lutyens as consulting architect; opened 3 July 1933 by the Prince of Wales on the same day as Twickenham and Chiswick bridges. Three wide reinforced concrete arches faced in red brick and Portland stone to complement Hampton Court Palace opposite. Carries the A309 between East Molesey (Surrey) and Hampton Court. Grade II listed 1952; maintained by Surrey County Council. Structurally a concrete arch; kind set to concrete_beam as the nearest category (?). Length, width and deck height approximate (?).

name: Queen Elizabeth II Bridge (Dartford Crossing)
notes: OUTSIDE FRAME - about 30 km downstream of the Thames Barrier, far east of the Hampton Court to Barrier study area; included only for completeness. Cable-stayed bridge designed by Hellmut Homberg with Halcrow as check engineer, opened by Elizabeth II on 30 October 1991 at a cost of GBP 120 million. Main span 450 m, towers 137 m high, deck about 61 m above water at the crown - deck_height_m 57.5 is a mid-span average (?). Carries four southbound lanes of the A282/M25; northbound traffic uses the two tunnels. Length 812 m is the cable-stayed structure; the whole crossing including approach viaducts is about 2,872 m (?). Structurally cable-stayed; kind set to suspension as the nearest category (?).
